newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition appeals for street protests.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition appeals for street protests.

text.p: Serbian opposition parties urged supporters on Wednesday to protest in the streets to defend a victory in local elections and accused the authorities of trying to annul the results through massive fraud.
Electoral officials on Tuesday confirmed the opposition's victory in the capital Belgrade, a stunning blow to the ruling Socialists led by President Slobodan Milosevic.
But authorities had failed to verify voting results by Tuesday evening as required by law in several other major towns where the opposition said it scored majorities against the Socialists.

As tensions mounted, the three leaders of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition and other opposition members of parliament announced a hunger strike at 6:30 p.m. (1730 GMT), demanding the Socialists accept their defeat.

The 66 opposition representatives said they would stay on the fifth floor of the Serbian parliament in Belgrade "until the democratically expressed desires of the people are fulfilled," said a coalition statement.
Zajedno appealed for supporters to demonstrate in front of the parliament in the city centre to back their demands.

"In practically all towns in Serbia where we have won results are being cancelled, exactly to the extent it is necessary to cancel our victory and to give it to those who have lost the elections," Zoran Djindjic, head of the opposition Democratic Party, told reporters earlier.
Djindjic and other opposition leaders called on their councillors to enter municipal assemblies and form new local governments.
Electoral commissions by law were required to confirm official results by Tuesday evening, 48 hours after polling stations closed.
But the commissions have cited unspecified irregularities in various municipalities where the opposition won a majority and said another round of voting was required.

"Such an illegal situation and attempt to reverse the will of the people is leading to a destabilisation of the state and the consequences could be very dramatic," said Vesna Pesic, head of the opposition Civic Alliance,
The coalition later warned that Socialist authorities were preparing the ground to declare a state of emergency.
"The clear intention of the (Socialist party) to annul the election results is an introduction to a state of emergency in Serbia," an opposition statement said.

In the southern town of Nis, the local electoral commission announced that the ruling Socialists had won an additional 11 seats in the city assembly due to alleged irregularities, the Tanjug state news agency reported.
The opposition says it has election material showing they won a majority of 41 out of 70 seats in the Nis assembly.
Some 30,000 protested in the centre of Nis on Tuesday night and special riot police were sent in to guard the city hall.
More demonstrations were launched in other towns on Wednesday evening.
In the central town of Kraljevo, several thousand people gathered in the main square, demanding an answer from the electoral commission, an opposition spokesman said by telephone.
Earlier, Zajedno leaders met diplomats from the United States and European Union countries and showed them election material which they said proved their victory was legitimate.
Opposition coalition officials said privately they received no pledges from Western powers to press Milosevic's government over the election.

They said diplomats view Milosevic as an important guarantor of stability in the region after he signed a peace agreement ending four years of war in the former Yugoslav republics of Bosnia and Croatia.
"We know we have to fight our own battles," said one opposition official.
